structure: Gig dispatch: one match between a driver, the dispatch platform and a rider

parties.label: D
parties.name: driver
parties.active: 1 = the driver is available in the zone and goes when a trip is shown; 0 = waiting. This collapses location, eligibility and the accept decision into one bit.

parties.label: P
parties.name: dispatch platform
parties.active: 1 = a trip is assigned and shown to the parties; 0 = no assignment. This collapses matching, pricing and notification into one bit.

parties.label: R
parties.name: rider
parties.active: 1 = the rider has requested and confirmed a ride, then waits at the curb; 0 = no live request. This collapses opening the app, requesting, confirming and waiting into one bit.

encodings.account: The platform's operations manual: the system commits on a joint condition of driver availability and rider confirmation.

P.quote: The system assigns a trip only when an eligible driver is available and a rider has confirmed the request; the assignment is binding on both and sets the fare.

D.quote: When the trip comes up I go. If nothing comes up I wait.

R.quote: Once it says a driver is assigned, I wait at the curb.

P.why: The drivers' account in ¶3 says the app only conveys what the driver sets. The evidence does not settle which account is right, so it is encoded as a separate rival.

R.why: One rider in ¶6 texts a regular driver when the app is slow. This is a single unsupported claim, and other cities ban off-app arrangements. It is recorded as an alternative, not an edge.

D.why: The same ¶6 off-app contact would let a driver act on a rider directly. Only some drivers and riders do this, and no log or agreement among the parties documents it.

predicted.reason: The platform's rule is an AND of driver and rider that neither party can compute alone, and both parties then read the platform's output, so the loop through the mediator should not reduce to pairwise links.

encodings.account: The drivers' account: the app conveys a signal the driver sets and follows what the driver does.

P.quote: The app just pings me with whatever is nearby. I decide. It's a suggestion, it follows what I do.

D.quote: When the trip comes up I go. If nothing comes up I wait.

R.quote: Once it says a driver is assigned, I wait at the curb.

P.why: The manual in ¶2 says assignment requires rider confirmation and is binding. A single driver's description does not rule this out, and it is encoded as the other rival.

R.why: One rider in ¶6 texts a regular driver when the app is slow. This is a single unsupported claim, not an edge.

predicted.reason: If the platform only relays the driver's state, the driver and platform form a two-party loop, and the rider only reads the platform's output without feeding back into anyone.

encodings.account: Several idle drivers in one zone are interchangeable candidates, and the platform commits when any one eligible driver and a confirmed rider are present. Each driver acts when a trip is shown, and the rider acts when told a driver is assigned.

P.quote: The system assigns a trip only when an eligible driver is available and a rider has confirmed the request
Any eligible driver in range may be assigned.

D1.quote: When the trip comes up I go. If nothing comes up I wait.

D2.quote: When the trip comes up I go. If nothing comes up I wait.
In dense hours several drivers are idle in the same zone.

R.quote: Once it says a driver is assigned, I wait at the curb.

P.why: Under the drivers' account in ¶3, the platform only relays whichever driver is nearby: "The app just pings me with whatever is nearby." That reading drops the rider's confirmation from the platform's rule.

predicted.reason: P is active only when some driver and the rider are both active, so neither side reaches the other without P. The driver pool adds substitutes on the driver side but leaves the platform in the middle. The two drivers should enter the core together as interchangeable members, with P and R.

encodings.account: Drivers and riders who have each other's numbers can arrange a trip directly. The platform is one route to a match, and the direct tie replaces it when the app fails. Where off-app contact is banned, this tie does not exist, so this reading holds only for the cities with contact.

P.quote: the assignment is binding on both and sets the fare

D.quote: Some drivers and riders exchange numbers and arrange repeat trips directly.
When the trip comes up I go. If nothing comes up I wait.

R.quote: If the app is slow I just text my regular driver.
Once it says a driver is assigned, I wait at the curb.

P.why: The drivers' account in ¶3 treats the platform as following the driver: "It's a suggestion, it follows what I do."

predicted.reason: The direct tie lets D and R each be active without P, and each stays active if the other is. The pair D-R sustains itself, so P drops out of the core. The match no longer depends on the mediator.

not_permitted.why: The drafts already hold the two readings the text supports, which are the manual's commit in ¶2 and the driver's suggestion in ¶3. No passage supports a third, such as the platform following the rider alone.

not_permitted.reading: Direct tie as a complement (D or R needs both P and the other party)
not_permitted.why: ¶6 says "If the app is slow I just text my regular driver". The rider goes around the app instead of needing it as well, so the tie is a substitute. No passage says the parties need the mediator in addition to the direct contact.

not_permitted.reading: Direct tie present for all drivers and riders
not_permitted.why: ¶6 says "Other cities ban off-app arrangements and drivers there have no way to reach riders except through the platform." In those cities the direct tie is absent, so the substitute encoding cannot be applied across all cities.
